titulo: What Is AI, Really? It's Just a File of Numbers
descripcion: There's no rulebook inside an AI. Just a file of 405 billion numbers that predicts one word-piece at a time. Here's what's really happening when a chatbot answers you: tokens, next-token prediction, training on 15 trillion tokens, why it runs on GPUs, why it doesn't remember you, and why it makes things up.

escenas.texto: Somewhere right now, a computer is holding a file.
It isn't an app. It isn't a list of instructions. It's eight hundred and ten gigabytes of numbers, and nothing else.
And yet, when you type a question, those numbers answer you. They write essays, fix broken code, and explain black holes.
So what is actually going on in there? Is it thinking? Is it some kind of operating system? Let's open the file.
Chapter one. It's not a program. At least, not the way you think.
A normal program is written by people, line by line. If this happens, do that. Every single rule was typed by a programmer.

visual.etiqueta: every rule typed by a person

escenas.texto: An operating system, like Windows or Android, is the same idea on a massive scale. It manages your memory, your files and your apps, with rules that humans wrote.

visual.titulo: AN OPERATING SYSTEM = RULES HUMANS WROTE

escenas.texto: A modern AI model is different. Nobody wrote its rules. In fact, nobody fully understands what most of them are.
What it has instead is a giant table of numbers, called weights, or parameters. Meta's Llama three point one, one of the biggest open models ever released, has four hundred and five billion of them.

visual.label: parameters in Llama 3.1 405B
visual.note: each one is just a number

escenas.texto: Each of those numbers takes two bytes to store. Do the math, and you get that eight hundred and ten gigabyte file.
The program that actually runs the model is tiny by comparison. Simple working versions have been written in around a thousand lines of code. Almost all of the intelligence lives in the numbers.
So here's a better picture. The model is not an operating system. It's more like a movie, and the code is the video player. The player is simple. The movie is where everything happens.
Chapter two. How it reads.
Here's the first surprise. The model never sees letters or words. It only sees numbers.

visual.pre: it never sees letters or words

escenas.texto: Before your message goes in, it gets chopped into pieces called tokens. A token is often a short word, or part of a longer one.

visual.frase: The cat sat on the mat.

escenas.texto: A word like unbelievable might be split into three pieces: un, believ, able.
Then each piece is swapped for an ID number from a fixed dictionary. Llama three's dictionary has about a hundred and twenty eight thousand entries.

visual.nota: vocabulary: ~128,000 tokens · IDs shown are illustrative

escenas.texto: On average, one token is about three quarters of an English word. So the whole script of this video is less than two thousand tokens.
Chapter three. The only job.
Now the numbers flow through the model, and here's the part that sounds too simple to be true. The model has exactly one job: guess the next token.
Give it, the cat sat on the. It doesn't look the answer up. It gives a score to every token in its dictionary. Mat scores high. Floor and couch get a little. Banana gets almost nothing.
Then it picks one, adds it to the sentence, and starts over, predicting the token after that. And again. And again. One piece at a time.
That's what you're watching when a chatbot types out its answer. It isn't revealing a finished thought. It's predicting the reply live, piece by piece.
And every piece is expensive. For a model with four hundred and five billion parameters, one token takes roughly eight hundred billion arithmetic operations.
Inside, the numbers pass through layer after layer. The biggest Llama has a hundred and twenty six of them. Each layer reshapes the meaning a little more, until the last one produces those scores.
Somewhere in all that multiplying, things that look a lot like grammar, facts and reasoning show up. Nobody programmed them. They emerged.
Chapter four. Where did the numbers come from?
At the very beginning, the weights are random. A brand new model is pure noise. Ask it anything and you get gibberish.
Then comes training. You show it real text, hide the next token, and make it guess.

visual.nota: hide the next token · make it guess

escenas.texto: When it guesses wrong, a bit of calculus works out which way to nudge every single weight, so the right answer becomes slightly more likely. Then it does it again. Trillions of times.
Llama three was trained on more than fifteen trillion tokens. That's roughly a hundred million books' worth of text.
For the biggest version, Meta used over sixteen thousand Nvidia H one hundred chips. In total, about thirty one million GPU hours.
A single chip working alone would need about three and a half thousand years to do the same job.
After that comes a second, smaller stage. People write example conversations and rate the model's answers, so it learns to behave like a helpful assistant, instead of just continuing random text.

items.texto: It learns to act like an assistant

escenas.texto: And then, training stops. The numbers are frozen. That frozen file is what you talk to.
Chapter five. Why AI runs on graphics cards.
Almost all of that work is one tiny operation, repeated an absurd number of times. Multiply two numbers, add the result to a running total.

visual.tex: a_1 w_1 + a_2 w_2 + a_3 w_3 + \cdots

escenas.texto: A regular processor has a handful of powerful cores. It's brilliant at doing different things, one after another.
A graphics card has thousands of simpler cores. An H one hundred has almost seventeen thousand. They all do the same simple math at the same time, and that's exactly what a neural network needs.
Memory matters just as much. One H one hundred holds eighty gigabytes. The full Llama model, at sixteen bits, doesn't fit even in ten of them.

visual.note: more than 10 GPUs just to hold it

escenas.texto: Chapter six. Does it remember you?
Here's something most people get wrong. When you chat with an AI, it isn't learning from you. The weights don't change. Not a single number.

visual.pre: while you chat, the weights are

escenas.texto: So how does it remember what you said five messages ago? Every time you send something, the entire conversation is fed back in, from the very top.

visual.etiqueta: the whole chat, every single time

mensajes.texto: A region where gravity traps light...
Billions of times the Sun's mass...
Wait, what did I ask first?

escenas.texto: That text is called the context window. It's the model's short term memory. Llama three point one can hold about a hundred and twenty eight thousand tokens at once. When a chat gets longer than that, the oldest part simply falls out. It isn't forgotten. It was never stored.
Features that look like long term memory usually work the same way. Saved notes get pasted into the context before your message. The model itself still learns nothing.

items.texto: Notes are saved outside the model

escenas.texto: Chapter seven. Why it makes things up.
Remember the one job: predict a likely next token. Likely. Not true.
Most of the time, likely and true are the same thing, because most of the training text was right.

But ask about something rare, like an obscure paper or a tiny town, and the scores come out almost flat. The model still has to pick something, and it writes it in the same fluent, confident tone. That's a hallucination.
There's no fact checker hidden inside the file. Newer systems reduce the problem by letting the model search the web or check sources, but underneath, it's still a prediction machine.
So, what is AI, really?

It's a file of numbers, shaped by trillions of guesses. A small program loads it onto powerful chips. Your words become tokens, the tokens flow through more than a hundred layers, and out comes a guess for the next piece. Repeated fast enough to feel like a conversation.

visual.titulo: A FILE OF NUMBERS + A SMALL PROGRAM + FAST CHIPS

escenas.texto: Not an operating system. Not a brain in a box. Something genuinely new: a compressed echo of almost everything people have written.

visual.pre: not an OS · not a brain in a box
